Burnt
BURNT
p.p. / adj.
Past participle of burn, Old English beornan / bærnan: to be on fire, to consume with fire. Webster 1828: consumed, scorched, heated, subjected to the action of fire. In the KJV the ordinary sacred cluster is the burnt offering / burnt sacrifice — the whole given to the flame. The companion entry burnt-offering treats the institution; this page is the participle and the KJV word burnt itself.

Biblical Definition

Burnt in Scripture is fire that finishes the gift. Noah’s first altar after the flood is this: he offered burnt offerings on the altar (Gen 8:20). The law’s first offering is the same: the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD (Lev 1:9). Abraham is told to offer Isaac for a burnt offering (Gen 22:2) — the whole son, not a portion — and the ram is provided in his stead. The Hebrew name of the rite is already treated at burnt-offering; the English participle tells the manner: nothing held back from the flame. That is why the prophets can say God is full of burnt offerings when the heart is not His (Isa 1:11), and why Samuel can say to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). Hebrews reads the whole Levitical flame as shadow: In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure (Heb 10:6), because the body of Christ is the offering God did appoint. Psalm 51 holds both ends without cheating: the broken spirit now, and the restored altar later — thou delightest not in burnt offering while the bones are still unhealed (Ps 51:16), yet burnt offering returns when Zion is built. The dictionary therefore refuses two reductions. Burnt is not a mood of exhaustion, and it is not a technique for buying God. It is whole consumption, fulfilled in the Son who gave Himself an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour (Eph 5:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BURNT as the participle passive of burn: consumed; scorched; heated; subjected to the action of fire.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 1:9 — "But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD."

Genesis 22:2 — "And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of."

Psalm 51:16 — "For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering."

Hebrews 10:6 — "In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure."

Isaiah 1:11 — "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats."

Modern Corruption

Burnt is corrupted when the whole-offering is recast as burnout and self-care, when ritual fire is treated as a bribe that excuses disobedience, and when the cross is reduced to inspirational self-gift without penal substitution.

expand to see more

Therapeutic English has stolen the participle and aimed it at the nerves. “Burnt out.” “Burned.” The recovery is not to deny exhaustion as a creaturely limit; it is to refuse the swap. Leviticus 1 is not a wellness crash. It is a whole animal on a real altar, a sweet savour unto the LORD. The church that talks more about burnout than about burnt offering has changed religions.

The second corruption is ritualism without obedience. Isaiah 1 and 1 Samuel 15 already named it: God is full of burnt offerings when the hands are full of blood and the ears are shut. High-church aesthetic, low-church busywork, and every scheme that treats giving, singing, or attending as a substitute for repentance repeat Saul at Gilgal. To obey is better than sacrifice. The flame does not launder rebellion.

The third corruption is to empty Hebrews 10. Liberal Protestantism makes the burnt offerings a primitive stage the race outgrew; some evangelical registers make the cross a display of love without wrath, a self-gift without substitution. The epistle says the contrary: God had no pleasure in those offerings because He prepared a body for the Son. The burnt thing is fulfilled, not discarded, in Christ’s once-for-all offering. Penal substitution is not a later theory laid on the text. It is why the fire had to finish the gift.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English beornan / bærnan, to burn. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Hebrew ‘ōlāh (H5930) at Ps 51:16 and Isa 1:11; Greek holokautōma (G3646) at Heb 10:6. Leviticus 1:9 and Genesis 22:2 are untagged in this cache; no Hebrew number is invented for them. The institution is treated at the existing burnt-offering entry; this page does not mint a second number.

expand to see more

Hebrew ‘ōlāh (H5930) — burnt offering, that which goes up in smoke (Ps 51:16; Isa 1:11).

Greek holokautōma (G3646) — whole burnt offering (Heb 10:6, In burnt offerings … thou hast had no pleasure).

Old English beornan / bærnan — to be on fire; the English participle the KJV uses for what the flame finished.

Companion entry burnt-offering already holds the rite; this page is the participle burnt, not a newly guessed Strong’s for every untagged OT occurrence.

Usage

"A burnt sacrifice is the whole given to the flame — Noah after the flood, the law at the door of the tent, Isaac named and the ram provided."

"God may be full of burnt offerings and still refuse them when the heart is shut (Isa 1:11; 1 Sam 15:22)."

"Hebrews 10:6 reads the Levitical flame as shadow; the body of Christ is the offering God appointed."
